notes_to_keep: 'lossy-trapdoor-function' has no page; it lives only as a section of [[trapdoor-permutation]].
pages.wrong_reason: Lossy trapdoor functions are not known to imply trapdoor permutations. The injective branch of a lossy TDF is an injective trapdoor FUNCTION, not a permutation: in the Peikert-Waters constructions (STOC 2008, 'Lossy Trapdoor Functions and Their Applications', eprint 2007/279) the domain and range differ, and no construction of TDPs from lossy TDFs exists in the literature. The migrated sentence conflates injective TDFs with TDPs, exactly as flagged in .reductions/suspected-errors.json for content/Primitives/trapdoor-permutation.md line 50 (affectsEdges red-ltf-to-tp). The correct edges are: lossy TDF => injective trapdoor function, and lossy TDF => IND-CCA-secure PKE, both due to Peikert-Waters; a PW08 reference page would need to be created for them.

Replacement edges (LTDF => injective TDF, LTDF => CCA-secure PKE) need a PW08 reference page: Chris Peikert, Brent Waters, 'Lossy Trapdoor Functions and Their Applications', STOC 2008 (also SIAM J. Comput. 40(6), 2011), https://eprint.iacr.org/2007/279 — not yet verified online in this pass because eprint is egress-blocked; verify before creating.
The source prose on trapdoor-permutation.md should also be fixed (skeptical-checker lane).

pages.wrong_reason: A low-complexity PRG alone is not known to imply iO, and JLS21 does not claim it does. The migrated bullet says the PRG 'is required by' the JLS21 construction — a necessary-ingredient statement, not a reduction. JLS21's theorem is conjunctive: sub-exponential hardness of (1) SXDH on asymmetric bilinear groups of prime order, (2) LWE over Z_p with subexponential modulus-to-noise ratio, (3) LPN over Z_p with inverse-polynomial error rate, and (4) the existence of a Boolean PRG in NC^0 (not NC^1) with stretch n^{1+tau}. Verified against the eprint 2020/1003 / STOC 2021 theorem statement (via web search; eprint direct fetch egress-blocked). The correct four-hypothesis hyperedge already exists as content/Reductions/ddh-and-lpn-and-lwe-and-nc1-prg-to-io-jls21.md (which itself needs DDH -> SXDH and NC^1 -> NC^0 corrections, as its own notes record). This single-hypothesis page should be deleted or absorbed into that page.
flags: Recommend deleting this page in favor of the four-hypothesis JLS21 edge (ddh-and-lpn-and-lwe-and-nc1-prg-to-io-jls21).

JLS21's PRG hypothesis is a Boolean PRG in NC^0 with polynomial stretch, not NC^1; the wiki's JLS21 reference-page abstract is itself a paraphrase containing the same NC^1/DDH errors and should be replaced with the real abstract (reference-fixer lane).

pages.wrong_reason: The hypothesis set omits a load-bearing assumption: JLS21 additionally assumes sub-exponential SXDH on asymmetric bilinear (pairing) groups. {sub-exponential LWE, LPN, PRG} without any bilinear-group assumption is not known to imply iO — every known well-founded iO construction uses a pairing assumption (JLS21 uses SXDH; the follow-up JLS22, eprint 2021/1334, removes LWE but uses DLIN). Also, the PRG in JLS21 is a Boolean PRG in NC^0 (not NC^1) with stretch n^{1+tau}, and the LPN is over Z_p with error rate 1/l^delta. Verified against the eprint 2020/1003 / STOC 2021 theorem statement via web search. The correct four-hypothesis edge already exists as content/Reductions/ddh-and-lpn-and-lwe-and-nc1-prg-to-io-jls21.md (itself needing DDH -> SXDH and NC^1 -> NC^0 corrections). This three-hypothesis page is an incomplete duplicate and should be deleted or merged into it.

sources.ref_file_title: Ale03 - More on average case vs approximation complexity
sources.note: Existing wiki reference page; cryptobib_key FOCS:Alekhnovich03.

pages.class_justification: Alekhnovich's construction uses LPN samples generically (the public key is an LPN sample; encryption combines further samples), and the security proof is a straightline reduction that runs any CPA distinguisher as an oracle to distinguish LPN samples from uniform. Fixed construction, fixed reduction, adversary used only as an oracle — the fully-black-box shape.
pages.statement: [[learning-parity-with-noise#noise-level|Mid-noise LPN]] with noise rate $\varepsilon = \Theta(1/\sqrt{k})$ implies CPA-secure [[public-key-encryption|PKE]] [[Ale03 - More on average case vs approximation complexity|Ale03]]. The noise regime is essential: PKE from constant-noise LPN with polynomial hardness remains open.
pages.sketch: Alekhnovich's bit encryption: the public key is an LPN sample $(\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{s}+\mathbf{e})$ with $\sqrt{m}$-sparse noise; a ciphertext masks the plaintext bit with $\mathbf{r}^{\top}\mathbf{b}$ for a fresh sparse $\mathbf{r}$, sending $(\mathbf{r}^{\top}\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{r}^{\top}\mathbf{b} + \beta)$. Decryption uses $\mathbf{s}$ to strip $\mathbf{r}^{\top}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{s}$, leaving $\mathbf{r}^{\top}\mathbf{e} + \beta$; the inner product of two $\sqrt{m}$-sparse vectors is biased toward $0$, so the bit is recovered with constant advantage and correctness is amplified by repetition.
notes_to_keep: The noise regime is part of the assumption's identity; the flat hypothesis identifier lpn should become the mid-noise variant.
flags: DUPLICATE: content/Reductions/noise-level-to-pke-ale03.md (batch red-19) records the same edge with hypothesis lpn-mid-noise and source Ale03. Recommend keeping one page (the regime-qualified one) and deleting this flat-hypothesis duplicate.

The frontmatter hypothesis [lpn] overstates the claim: unqualified (constant-noise, polynomial-hardness) LPN => PKE is a major open problem. The wiki already records the sub-exponential constant-noise route separately (subexponential-lpn-to-pke-yz16).

sources.ref_file_title: CIMR25 - Secret-Key PIR from Random Linear Codes
sources.authors: Caicai Chen, Yuval Ishai, Tamer Mour, Alon Rosen
sources.note: Now published at STOC 2026 (doi 10.1145/3798129.3800906); the wiki reference page still says venue: preprint.

sources.ref_file_title: BM26 - Secret-Key PIR from One-Way Functions
sources.note: Weakens the assumption to any one-way function, at the cost of higher communication.

pages.statement: For all constants $\gamma, \varepsilon > 0$, hardness of [[learning-parity-with-noise|LPN]] with noise rate $k^{-\gamma}$ implies secret-key PIR ([[single-server-private-information-retrieval#secret-key-pir-sk-pir|SK-PIR]]) with $O(N^{\varepsilon})$ communication and $\poly(N)$ server storage for an $N$-bit database [[CIMR25 - Secret-Key PIR from Random Linear Codes|CIMR25]]. For $\gamma < 1/2$ the hypothesis lies in a regime not known to imply public-key encryption, giving evidence that PKE is not necessary for SK-PIR.
pages.improvements_text: - SK-PIR with online communication $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{N})$ follows from one-way functions alone — [[BM26 - Secret-Key PIR from One-Way Functions|BM26]]
notes_to_keep: The LPN noise regime (rate $k^{-\gamma}$ with $\gamma < 1/2$) is load-bearing: it places SK-PIR below the PKE threshold, which is the paper's main point.
flags: CIMR25 is now published at STOC 2026; the wiki reference page's venue field says preprint (reference-fixer lane).

The CIMR25 reference page's Notes attribute the LSN conjecture's introduction to CIMR25; Learning Subspace with Noise was introduced by DKL09 (as the page itself suspects at its 'Wait actually' line). Affects the LSN edges (red-17), not this one.

sources.ref_file_title: CIMR25 - Secret-Key PIR from Random Linear Codes
sources.authors: Caicai Chen, Yuval Ishai, Tamer Mour, Alon Rosen

pages.statement: Hardness of [[learning-parity-with-noise#noise-level|high-noise LPN]] (noise rate $k^{-\gamma}$ for a constant $0 < \gamma < 1/2$, a regime not known to imply public-key encryption) implies secret-key [[doubly-efficient-pir|DEPIR]] in a weak sense: for any constant $\varepsilon > 0$, communication is $O(N^{\varepsilon})$ and, with server storage $N^{1+\varepsilon}$, the server reads only $N/\mathrm{polylog}(N)$ bits of the encoded database per query [[CIMR25 - Secret-Key PIR from Random Linear Codes|CIMR25]]. Server work is sublinear only by a polylogarithmic factor.
flags: The DEPIR label is generous: CIMR25 itself calls the $N/\mathrm{polylog}(N)$-probe scheme 'a very weak form of doubly efficient sk-PIR'. It meets the wiki's DEPIR definition (communication and query-time computation o(N)) only barely; a human should confirm the exact theorem parameters against the paper (eprint direct fetch was egress-blocked; theorem shape confirmed via web search of the PDF).

This page (high-noise) and noise-level-to-depir-cimr25 (mid-noise) record one CIMR25 theorem, which holds for every constant gamma > 0, split across the wiki's two overlapping regimes; the split follows the one-hypothesis-per-sufficient-assumption rule, but the wiki's mid-noise range (gamma < 1) strictly contains high-noise (gamma < 1/2), so consider a single regime-parameterized page.

sources.ref_file_title: BLVW19 - Worst-Case Hardness for LPN and Cryptographic Hashing via Code Smoothing
sources.authors: Zvika Brakerski, Vadim Lyubashevsky, Vinod Vaikuntanathan, Daniel Wichs
sources.note: Existing wiki reference page; cryptobib_key EC:BLVW19. Abstract confirms: LPN with noise rate log^2(n)/n implies collision resistant hash functions.

sources.ref_file_title: YZW+19 - Collision Resistant Hashing from Sub-exponential Learning Parity with Noise
sources.authors: Yu Yu, Jiang Zhang, Jian Weng, Chun Guo, Xiangxue Li
sources.note: Concurrent work; different LPN regimes (sub-exponential constant-noise or 1/sqrt(n)-noise), via the bSVP framework.

pages.statement: [[learning-parity-with-noise#noise-level|Low-noise LPN]] with noise rate $\log^2(k)/k$ implies [[hash-function#collision-resistance|collision-resistant hash functions]] [[BLVW19 - Worst-Case Hardness for LPN and Cryptographic Hashing via Code Smoothing|BLVW19]].
pages.sketch: The hash family is $h_{\mathbf{A}}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$ restricted to low-Hamming-weight inputs, which compresses by an entropy count; a collision yields a low-weight vector in the kernel of $\mathbf{A}$, and BLVW19 show via a code-smoothing argument that finding such vectors breaks LPN at noise rate $\log^2(k)/k$.
pages.improvements_text: - Concurrent work obtains collision-resistant hashing from constant-noise LPN with $2^{n^{1/2+\varepsilon}}$ hardness, or from noise rate $1/\sqrt{n}$ with $2^{\Omega(\sqrt{n}/\log n)}$ hardness, via the binary-SVP framework — [[YZW+19 - Collision Resistant Hashing from Sub-exponential Learning Parity with Noise|YZW+19]]
notes_to_keep: YZW+19's hypotheses are sub-exponential-hardness LPN regimes (constant-noise or noise rate $1/\sqrt{n}$), not the $\log^2(k)/k$ regime; it arguably belongs on a separate edge from the subexponential-lpn variant.
flags: CONCLUSION UPGRADE: the migrated bullet says OWF, but both cited papers prove collision-resistant hashing; the conclusion should be the crhf variant (hash-function#collision-resistance), not one-wayness. LPN in essentially any regime implies OWF trivially, so as written the page cited two strong results for a trivial claim.
If a verifier prefers strict one-source-per-edge, move YZW+19 to its own subexponential-lpn => CRHF page instead of the improvement bullet.

pages.class_justification: One fixed sample transformation (add independent Bernoulli noise to each label) and one fixed reduction that runs the constant-noise distinguisher once as an oracle on the transformed samples; the transformation maps rate-epsilon LPN samples exactly to rate-epsilon' LPN samples with the same secret and maps uniform to uniform, so advantage is preserved exactly. This is the fully-black-box shape.
pages.statement: If $(k,\varepsilon)$-[[learning-parity-with-noise|LPN]] is hard for noise rate $\varepsilon = \log^c(k)/k$ (the low-noise regime), then $(k,\varepsilon')$-LPN is hard for every constant $\varepsilon' \in (\varepsilon, 1/2)$ (in particular the constant-noise regime): LPN hardness is monotone under increasing the noise rate — folklore.
pages.sketch: Given a sample $(\mathbf{a}, b)$, output $(\mathbf{a}, b + e')$ for fresh $e' \getsr \mathrm{Ber}(\tau)$ with $\varepsilon(1-\tau) + \tau(1-\varepsilon) = \varepsilon'$. Rate-$\varepsilon$ LPN samples map exactly to rate-$\varepsilon'$ samples with the same secret, and uniform samples stay uniform, so any distinguisher for the noisier problem breaks the less-noisy one with the same advantage; the same transformation preserves the secret, so it applies to search LPN as well.
notes_to_keep: Naming on the LPN page is counterintuitive: the high-noise regime has strictly less noise than the constant-noise regime.

SUSPECTED DEFINITION ERROR on the LPN page (also in suspected-errors.json): the mid-noise range ($\gamma < 1$) strictly contains the high-noise range ($\gamma < 1/2$), so the regimes are not disjoint as presented.
flags: Page title 'Noise Level => Noise Level' is uninformative; it should name the regimes (e.g. 'Low-noise LPN => Constant-noise LPN'). The same monotonicity gives every step low => mid => high => constant; if the wiki wants the full chain, each link is this same folklore reduction.

Direction verified: low-noise (strongest) implies constant-noise (weakest); a constant-noise adversary is turned into a low-noise adversary by noise padding. Matches the page's hypotheses/conclusion as recorded.
